reference.source: Tachdjian's Pediatric Orthopaedics / Campbell's Operative Orthopaedics
clinicalPearls: A traction apophysitis of the calcaneal (heel) apophysis rather than a true osteonecrosis
Affected site is the posterior calcaneal apophysis at the insertion of the Achilles tendon
Typically affects active children roughly eight to fourteen years of age around a growth spurt, often bilaterally
Presents with activity-related posterior heel pain relieved by rest, with tenderness on medial-lateral squeeze of the heel
It is a clinical diagnosis; radiographs are usually obtained to exclude other causes rather than to confirm the condition
Sclerosis and fragmentation of the calcaneal apophysis is a normal developmental appearance and does not by itself establish the diagnosis
A positive squeeze test and tight gastrocnemius-soleus complex on examination support the diagnosis
Management is conservative with activity modification, heel cups or orthoses, calf and hamstring stretching and physiotherapy as needed
reference.pathophysiology: Sever disease is a traction apophysitis of the posterior calcaneal apophysis, arising where the powerful Achilles tendon inserts onto the still-cartilaginous growth centre of the heel. During periods of rapid growth the bones lengthen faster than the surrounding muscle-tendon units, increasing tension across the apophysis, while repetitive impact from running and jumping adds cyclical traction and compression. This repetitive microtrauma at the vulnerable cartilaginous apophysis produces inflammation and pain. The radiographic sclerosis and fragmentation often seen at the apophysis represent normal variation in ossification rather than avascular necrosis, and the condition resolves once the apophysis fuses at skeletal maturity.
additionalDifferentials: Achilles tendinopathy or insertional Achilles tendinitis
Osteomyelitis or bone tumour of the calcaneus
Tarsal coalition presenting with hindfoot pain
additionalInvestigations: Clinical squeeze (compression) test of the heel reproducing pain
Assessment of gastrocnemius-soleus tightness and ankle dorsiflexion
Plain radiographs primarily to exclude fracture, infection or tumour
Magnetic resonance imaging reserved for atypical, persistent or unilateral cases
Inflammatory markers if infection or inflammatory arthropathy is suspected
Gait and footwear assessment in the active child
redFlags: Rest pain, night pain or systemic features suggesting infection or malignancy
A discrete focal bony lesion or fracture line on imaging
Persistent unilateral pain not settling with conservative measures
Swelling, warmth or erythema over the heel pointing to an alternative diagnosis
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is excellent; symptoms are self-limiting and resolve with skeletal maturity as the apophysis fuses, with activity modification and stretching controlling pain in the interim and no long-term sequelae expected.
pitfalls: Interpreting the normal fragmented, sclerotic apophysis on radiographs as diagnostic or as osteonecrosis
Missing a calcaneal stress fracture, infection or tumour presenting as atypical heel pain
Failing to address tight calf musculature that perpetuates apophyseal traction
Complete immobilisation and deconditioning when relative activity modification would suffice
